title: Answer to Question: The Sri Lankan President's Announcement of His Government's Victory over the Tamil Fighters
text:
Answer to Question: The Sri Lankan President's Announcement of His Government's Victory over the Tamil Fighters

Question: On 19/5/2009 the Sri Lankan President Mahinda Rajapaksa announced on television the victory of his government over the Tamil Tiger fighters, saying: “Our homeland has been completely liberated from the separatist terrorists.” State television had shown the body of the commander of the Tamil Tiger fighters after the battles raging between the government and the Tamil Tigers had stopped. The Chief of Staff, General Sarath Fonseka, commented on this event by saying: “A few hours ago the body of the leader of the terrorists, Velupillai, who devastated the country, was found.” The President tried to calm the fears of the anxious Tamil population, as he said: “Our aim was to rescue the Tamil population from the grip of the rebels, and all of us must now live as equals in this free country.”

So what is the truth of the conflict in Sri Lanka? Is it a local conflict, a regional conflict or an international conflict? In whose favour was the outcome of this conflict? And can it be said that the conflict on the island has ended, or does it have later after-effects?

Answer:

To answer these questions we say:

1- The conflict raging between the Sri Lankan government and the Tamil Tiger fighters' movement has been described as the longest conflict. Its reality is that it is a conflict between America and Britain over control of the strategic Sri Lankan waters, and the conflict was being fed through the regional powers in the area, Pakistan and India.

2- The importance of Sri Lanka lies in its geographical location. Sri Lanka is 19 miles from the southern Indian coasts, i.e. it lies on one of the most important waterways connecting West Asia with its East. It is 22 miles from the narrowest point from the Indian subcontinent, which is called the Palk Strait. America has repeatedly sought to control the Palk Strait in order to turn it into an American military base to help it control the Indian Ocean and control the route of the oil of the Middle East and Africa which reaches China, and thereby limit China's ambitions of maritime extension towards the west. Directly after the attacks of the eleventh of September, the American Secretary of Defence Rumsfeld boarded the ship of consolidating American–Sri Lankan relations, since control of the Palk Strait threatens the waterway connecting India and its eastern states, which would force India to travel around Sri Lanka, meaning a lengthening of the travel distance to reach those states and a considerable increase in travel costs. Control of the Palk Strait also limits India's ambition as a regional state and limits its extension towards the east. This is what pushed China to strengthen its military relationship with the government of Sri Lanka and to supply it with weapons and military equipment. It is worth mentioning that India's failure to control the Palk Strait means that British interests in the region are affected; for hundreds of years Britain has sought to control the Indian Ocean in order to control the waterways in the region so as to supply the eastern markets with goods. In contrast, America's control over the Indian Ocean and over the Palk Strait harms Europe alongside Britain. That is, control over Sri Lanka is a very important aim for America, and it enables it to control the Chinese threats and to limit British and European influence in South Asia and the Near East.

3- The conflict began when Britain brought Tamil citizens from the Indian province of Tamil Nadu to work on the coffee and tea plantations, as it turned the island into a main plantation for the production of tea and coffee. But the Sinhalese Buddhist majority hated the racist British treatment, especially the preference of the Hindu Tamils over them. The independence of Sri Lanka from Britain in 1948 was a confirmation of the bitterness of the relationship between the two communities. The successive Sinhalese governments deliberately delayed granting appropriate political rights to the Tamils who live in the north of Sri Lanka, and for this reason the Tamils lost confidence in their political leaders and in the Sri Lankan political make-up, which never once did them justice. This was a cause of the emergence of many armed movements, the most famous of which is the Tamil Tigers movement, which was formed in 1976 under the leadership of its founder “Velupillai Prabhakaran”. The aim of the movement was to create an independent Tamil state named “Tamil Motherland” in the north and east of the island. The movement did not gain popular support until the eighties of the last century, especially after the failure of the attempt at constitutional reform in 1983.

The movement had been penetrated by agents of the English, the Indians and the Americans, which led to their being directed to fight the other armed movements. But Britain had the upper hand, especially in the eras of the Congress Party in India. In 1980 Britain pushed India to intervene in the issue of the Tamil Tigers movement and the Sri Lankan government, in response to the growing American influence on the island. This was under a cover that the Sri Lankan government accepted, namely preventing the Indian Tamils from joining the Tamils in the north of Sri Lanka to separate the north from the rest of the island, although the truth is that the Congress Party government in India at that time had noticed that the Sri Lankan army was on the verge of eliminating the Tamil Tigers movement. India's intervention continued outwardly in a political form, and in the form of support for the Tamil Tigers from behind a curtain, until the Indian government succeeded on 29/7/1987 in concluding a peace agreement between the Indian President Rajiv Gandhi and the Sri Lankan President Jayewardene. Because of this agreement the Sri Lankan government granted a set of privileges to the Tamils, among them involving the Tamil province in power, and allowing the presence of Indian peace forces, in return for India not supporting the armed Tamil movements.

4- India's failure to occupy part of Sri Lanka led to a humiliating withdrawal of the Indian forces. Then America exploited the feelings of hatred towards India to intervene between the Tamil Tigers movement and the Sri Lankan government. However, America preferred strengthening its relations with the government over strengthening them with the movement; therefore the relationship between America and the Sri Lankan government grew more, especially after the events of the eleventh of September. Then America recently gave the green light to the government to eliminate the Tamil Tigers within the framework of the global war on terror, and America also saw fit to build strong military and economic ties with Sri Lanka. In 2002 Washington managed to reach an agreement enabling American warships and fighter planes to use Sri Lankan territory, and in 2002 the American President Bush met the Sri Lankan Prime Minister “Wickremesinghe” in the White House and obtained an agreement for peace and economic development in Sri Lanka, and America and Sri Lanka signed a joint trade agreement (TIFA) in 2002. The biggest loser from this rapprochement between the two countries was Britain, which found itself isolated for two reasons. The first: the loss of the Indian Congress Party in the Indian elections and the victory of the Janata Party, which was opposed to adopting a position hostile to the American military and economic agreement with Sri Lanka. The second reason: that the Sri Lankan government came under American influence. That is, Britain's only option was to support the Tamil Tigers movement until it was recently eliminated.

5- America waited for the election of President Mahinda Rajapaksa as President of Sri Lanka in 2005 so as to guarantee the Sri Lankan government's support for eliminating the Tamil Tigers movement. In fact, Mahinda Rajapaksa's election campaign was on the basis of his promises to eliminate the Tamil Tigers movement, especially as Mahinda Rajapaksa had formed an alliance with the extremist party Janatha Vimukthi and with extremist Buddhist monks. America welcomed the re-election of Mahinda Rajapaksa, as the Deputy Spokesman of the American State Department, Adam Ereli, said at a press conference held in Washington: “We will continue to preserve the historic relationship of our two countries; we look forward to cooperation with President Mahinda Rajapaksa because he has confronted many specific challenges.” Through Mahinda Rajapaksa and his brother the Chief of Staff, America managed to eliminate the Tamil Tiger fighters. Because Britain, India and Europe grasped the step of America's agreement with Sri Lanka, they exerted every effort to prevent Mahinda Rajapaksa's government from eliminating the Tamil Tiger fighters.

6- America supported Mahinda Rajapaksa's government with effective weapons through Pakistan. In March 2006 Sri Lanka asked Pakistan to supply it with a missile-launching system when the Sri Lankan President Mahinda Rajapaksa visited Pakistan. In May 2008 the Sri Lankan Chief of Staff Fonseka concluded an agreement with Pakistan to buy 22 Pakistani tanks of the Al-Khalid type worth 100 million dollars, alongside the Pakistani authorities supplying Sri Lanka with a great deal of weapons worth 65 million dollars. On 19/1/2009, in a meeting that brought together the Pakistani Defence Minister Syed Athar Ali and his Sri Lankan counterpart Gotabaya Rajapaksa in Rawalpindi, the two sides agreed to strengthen military cooperation within the framework of joint military exercises and the exchange of intelligence information to combat terrorism.

7- When repeated victories against the Tamil Tigers were achieved, Britain and its agent India, alongside Europe, sought to accomplish a reconciliation between Mahinda Rajapaksa's government and the Tamil Tigers. Their aim in concluding the reconciliation was to prevent the elimination of the Tamil Tigers, and Britain and India were raising their voices, using the killing of Tamil civilians in the ongoing conflict as a pretext. Britain, India and Europe became active in the last days in urging a ceasefire, and encouraged Tamil demonstrators throughout the world to demonstrate against the killing of civilians by Mahinda Rajapaksa's government. As for America, it was playing with words about peace and a ceasefire, but it was encouraging the Sri Lankan government to reject that, and then supporting it by way of Pakistan. All of that made Mahinda Rajapaksa reject the offers of peace and a ceasefire. Thus the Sri Lankan government ignored those calls, and consequently it managed to crush the Tamil forces, that military organisation which controlled wide areas in the north of the island, controlled the police apparatus, and whose members boasted of their navy and their air force.

The defeat of the Tamil Tigers means that Indian and British influence in the north of the island has receded to a great extent, and this gave America the opportunity to strengthen its control over Sri Lanka and to establish permanent military bases in the country. It also provides the opportunity for America to control the Palk Strait and to intensify its naval presence in the Indian Ocean to confront the Chinese threats. Moreover, America can use Sri Lanka to pressure India – especially after the coming of the Congress Party in India for another five years of rule in India – to proceed in America's policies in the region once again. In any case, much awaits Mahinda Rajapaksa in repairing relations with the Tamils and accommodating their political demands, and because America is aware of that, it pre-empted the matter by supplying Mahinda Rajapaksa's government with aid through the International Monetary Fund to achieve those demands. For the stability of Sri Lanka is a vital interest for America, and a look at the history of the region shows that Britain and its agent India will work to build their influence in Sri Lanka anew. The Anglo-American conflict may have died down now, but it has not ended yet.

28 Jumada al-Ula 1430 AH

23/5/2009 CE
